title: GX Core overview (Great Expectations 1.x)
core_concepts: Data Source / Data Asset / Batch Definition
engineering_principles: Describe data with declarative, verifiable Expectations grouped into Suites; bind a Suite to a Batch Definition via a Validation Definition; run Validation Definitions in production through Checkpoints that trigger Actions; publish results as human-readable Data Docs. Workflows are programmatically defined in Python even though Expectations themselves form a declarative language.
practical_examples: Component chain Data Context -> Data Source -> Data Asset -> Batch Definition -> Expectation Suite -> Validation Definition -> Checkpoint -> Actions/Data Docs; the page shows version 1.24.1 of the 1.x line.
why_it_matters: Gives a schema framework a vocabulary for post-load content assertions (as opposed to DDL shape constraints) and a production pattern (Checkpoint + Actions) for alerting on validation failure.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation of the tool.
notes: Page does not describe metric history or anomaly detection; GX appears in the OpenLineage integrations list (see DQ-18).

title: dbt: Add data tests to your DAG
core_concepts: Generic data tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships)
Tests as SELECT queries returning failing rows
engineering_principles: A test is a SQL select that returns failing records; zero rows = pass. Generic tests should make up the bulk of the suite. Every model should have a primary-key test (unique + not_null). Tests run in the warehouse after the model is built; failures can be persisted for triage.
practical_examples: YAML: order_id -> unique, not_null; status -> accepted_values [placed, shipped, completed, returned]; customer_id -> relationships to ref('customers') field id. Singular test: select order_id, sum(amount) from fct_payments group by 1 having total_amount < 0.
why_it_matters: Defines the warehouse-test layer of the validation stack and codifies the minimum assertion (PK uniqueness/non-null) that a schema framework should require on every model.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with a visible last-updated date.
notes: Related dbt pages also fetched and verified: Unit tests (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/unit-tests, updated 2026-09-14; pre-build logic tests on static fixtures, CI/dev only, added v1.8); Sources with freshness warn_after/error_after and loaded_at_field (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/sources, updated 2026-09-16); Exposures with required owner name/email and type, maturity, depends_on (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/exposures, updated 2026-11-03); dbt-expectations package maintained by Metaplane, Apache-2.0, dbt >= 1.7, install pin 0.10.9 (https://github.com/metaplane/dbt-expectations, n.d.).

title: dbt: Model contracts
core_concepts: Constraints not_null, primary_key, foreign_key, unique, check
Definable-and-enforced vs definable-not-enforced vs not-definable per platform
Breaking-change detection against prior project state
Major version bump on backwards-incompatible change
engineering_principles: A contract is a set of upfront guarantees about a model's shape; dbt verifies query columns match the YAML and emits names/types/constraints into DDL so the platform enforces them at build time. Most analytical platforms only enforce not_null; Postgres enforces all five. Removing a column, changing a data_type, or removing/modifying a constraint on a contracted model is a breaking change requiring a major version bump.
practical_examples: YAML: models: dim_customers with config.contract.enforced: true, columns customer_id int (constraints: not_null), customer_name string. Supported for table, incremental (on_schema_change append_new_columns or fail) and view (names/types only); not Python models, materialized views, ephemeral, sources, seeds, snapshots.
why_it_matters: Directly answers where structural constraints are actually enforced: the OLTP database (Postgres) enforces PK/FK/UNIQUE/CHECK, analytical warehouses mostly do not, so DDL constraints must be the OLTP floor and warehouse tests must compensate downstream. Also supplies the breaking vs non-breaking classification for schema changes.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with last-updated date; the per-platform enforcement table is the authoritative statement for dbt adapters.
notes: The per-adapter table cells could not be attributed reliably from the fetched text except the explicit statements for Postgres (all five enforced) and Microsoft Fabric (only not_null checked).

title: Soda Core v4 (data quality and data contract verification engine)
core_concepts: soda contract verify (local, pipeline, Soda Cloud/Runner)
engineering_principles: Author checks declaratively in a YAML contract per dataset and verify schema and data with a CLI/Python API wherever the pipeline runs; the same contract can be published to Soda Cloud and verified remotely.
practical_examples: Contract with dataset-level schema and row_count checks and column-level missing/invalid checks; packages for Athena, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB, Fabric, PostgreSQL, Redshift, Snowflake, Spark DataFrames, SQL Server, Synapse, Trino. Docs home (also fetched, https://docs.soda.io/) shows a reconciliation check row_count_diff comparing a Snowflake orders dataset to a MySQL source with must_be_less_than: 1.
why_it_matters: Shows a YAML-declarative alternative to dbt tests that can run at ingestion or in the warehouse and that includes source-to-target reconciliation checks as first-class syntax.
authority_rationale: Official project README (vendor-maintained open source); less detailed than full docs, and the docs home page lacked technical depth.
notes: README no longer uses the name SodaCL; legacy v3 packages soda-core-{datasource} are pinned to 3.5.x. License type not stated in fetched text.

title: Deequ - Unit Tests for Data (AWS Labs)
organization_author: Amazon Web Services (awslabs); Schelter et al.
core_concepts: Anomaly detection on metrics over time
engineering_principles: Define unit tests for data as constraints over computed metrics (completeness, uniqueness, value sets, non-negativity, quantiles) and run them as Spark jobs; persist metrics so changes can be detected as anomalies; suggest constraints automatically for large datasets; compute metrics incrementally for growing/partitioned data.
practical_examples: Scala example over a five-row Item DataFrame checking size, completeness, uniqueness, allowed values, non-negativity, URL presence and median of numViews; reports productName 80% complete and only 40% of description values containing a URL. Deequ 2.x per-Spark-version artifacts (e.g., -spark-3.5); 2.1.0+ requires Java 11.
why_it_matters: Reference design for code-based, metrics-first validation at the Spark/ingestion layer and for storing quality metrics over time, which anomaly-based observability requires.
authority_rationale: Official AWS Labs project README backed by a peer-reviewed VLDB 2018 paper (Schelter et al., PVLDB 11(12), pp. 1781-1794).
notes: Apache-2.0 license.

title: Pandera documentation (0.35.0)
core_concepts: Lazy validation with SCHEMA vs DATA error report
Backends: pandas, PySpark SQL, Polars, Ibis, PyArrow, DataFusion; Narwhals backend
engineering_principles: Validate dataframes at runtime against statically declared schemas inside the pipeline code (at function boundaries via decorators), collect all violations lazily, and reuse schemas to synthesise test data.
practical_examples: schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({'column1': pa.Column(int, pa.Check.ge(0)), 'column2': pa.Column(float, pa.Check.lt(10)), 'column3': pa.Column(str, [pa.Check.isin([*'abc']), pa.Check(lambda s: s.str.len() == 1)])}); equivalent class Schema(pa.DataFrameModel) with pa.Field(ge=0) and @pa.check methods. Import from pandera.pandas (top-level import warns since v0.24.0).
why_it_matters: Represents the in-process, pre-write validation point (before data reaches a database or lake), complementing DDL constraints and warehouse tests.
authority_rationale: Official project documentation of a widely used open-source tool.
notes: Schema inference supported only on the pandas backend; feature support varies by backend.

title: Elementary - dbt-native data observability (OSS repository)
core_concepts: Anomaly detection tests as native dbt tests
Alerts to Slack and Microsoft Teams with owner tagging
Configuration as code in the dbt project
engineering_principles: Collect quality metrics via dbt tests, store dbt artifacts in the warehouse, detect anomalies in freshness/volume/column metrics, and route alerts to owners; use lineage with test results for impact and root-cause analysis.
practical_examples: OSS = Elementary dbt package + CLI that runs tests, detects anomalies and sends alerts; README attributes column-level lineage to Elementary Cloud; Cloud docs (https://docs.elementary-data.com/, also fetched) describe a metadata-only architecture ('We never access or process your raw data'), incidents and AI triage.
why_it_matters: Shows how observability can be implemented inside the warehouse-test layer with owner metadata driving alert routing, a requirement a schema framework must supply (owner per table).
authority_rationale: Official README of a reputable open-source tool; Apache-2.0; 2.4k stars; limited technical depth on the fetched pages.
notes: Anomaly-detection parameters (training period, sensitivity) were not retrievable from the fetched pages.

title: What is Data Observability? (Monte Carlo) [vendor]
core_concepts: Five pillars: freshness, quality, volume, schema, lineage
Data reliability engineering borrowing from SRE
engineering_principles: Treat data health like application health: monitor freshness (how up to date tables are), quality (NULL %, unique %, accepted ranges), volume (completeness), schema (who changed what, when) and lineage (affected upstream/downstream assets); measure data downtime (periods when data is partial, erroneous, missing or inaccurate) as the consumer-facing reliability metric.
practical_examples: Pillar descriptions with example signals; data downtime proposed as an SLA-like metric analogous to a SaaS product being up or down.
why_it_matters: Supplies the most widely cited taxonomy of observability signals, but it is vendor-originated and has changed (the updated page uses 'quality' where earlier versions used 'distribution'), so it should be treated as a taxonomy rather than a standard.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner/vendor post; marketing context; the author claims to have coined the term in 2019.
notes: Original URL https://www.montecarlodata.com/blog-what-is-data-observability/ now 301-redirects to montecarlo.ai. Vendor marketing; label accordingly.

title: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) v3.2.0
core_concepts: Sections: Fundamentals, Schema, References, Data quality, Support & communication channels, Pricing, Team, Roles, SLA, Infrastructure & servers, Authoritative definitions, Tags, Custom properties
engineering_principles: Express the contract for a dataset as platform-agnostic YAML carrying schema, quality rules, SLA, team/roles, servers and custom properties, validated by a published JSON Schema; the standard takes precedence over the companion schema in a conflict.
practical_examples: Repository links a full example (examples/all/full-example.odcs.yaml); IDE import instructions for IntelliJ and VS Code; docs site (https://bitol-io.github.io/open-data-contract-standard/latest/, also fetched) lists 15 sections including Context and Variables, each with its own page since v3.1.0.
why_it_matters: The single remaining open contract standard: PayPal's template evolved into it and the INNOQ Data Contract Specification has been deprecated in its favour, so a schema framework should target ODCS for cross-team dataset contracts.
authority_rationale: Open standard governed under the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation (Bitol project); citation on the page lists LF AI & Data Foundation, 2025.
notes: Lineage of the standard verified from two further fetched pages: PayPal data-contract-template (https://github.com/paypal/data-contract-template, Apache-2.0, README states it 'has evolved and is now called' ODCS under Bitol hosted by The Linux Foundation and AIDA User Group; not formally archived) and the Data Contract Specification v1.2.1 by Jochen Christ and Simon Harrer (https://github.com/datacontract/datacontract-specification, MIT) whose README deprecates DCS 'with the release of the Open Data Contract Standard v3.1.0', names ODCS the 'conceptual successor', keeps CLI support to end of 2026, and notes the Data Contract CLI can lint, test, import and export both formats. ODCS quality rule types and SLA property names were not enumerated on the fetched pages.

title: Schema Evolution and Compatibility for Schema Registry (Confluent Platform 8.4)
core_concepts: BACKWARD (default), BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, FORWARD, FORWARD_TRANSITIVE, FULL, FULL_TRANSITIVE, NONE
engineering_principles: Register every schema version and reject registrations that violate the configured compatibility mode. BACKWARD permits adding optional fields and removing fields (consumers upgrade first); FORWARD permits removing optional fields and adding fields (producers first); FULL permits only optional-field add/remove (independent upgrades); NONE disables checks. BACKWARD is preferred for Kafka so consumers can rewind to the start of a topic.
practical_examples: Compatibility table with allowed changes; per-subject REST configuration; note that Kafka Streams supports only BACKWARD-based modes and Confluent Cloud for Flink supports FULL, FULL_TRANSITIVE and BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE.
why_it_matters: Provides the precise, machine-enforced definition of breaking vs non-breaking schema change for streaming interfaces and the technical enforcement point for data contracts in event pipelines.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with last-updated date.
notes: Related Confluent page also fetched and verified: Kafka Connect Concepts (https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/connect/concepts.html, updated 2026-10-16) - dead letter queues apply only to sink connectors; errors.tolerance=none (default) fails the task, errors.tolerance=all skips silently so source vs processed record counts must be compared; errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name routes bad records; errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true adds _connect.errors.* headers explaining failures (default false).

title: Shifting Left: How Data Contracts Underpin People, Processes, and Technology [vendor blog]
organization_author: Confluent; Andrew Jones (author of 'Driving Data Quality with Data Contracts')
core_concepts: Data contract as human- and machine-readable metadata document
Schema, SLAs, documentation, categorisation, versioning and change management in the contract
Ownership by the data product owner
Publishing the contract to Schema Registry and applying it to a topic
engineering_principles: Handle quality, structure and governance at the point of data creation rather than after problems spread; codify schema and SLAs in a contract owned by the producer, publish it to the registry that both operational and analytical consumers use, and let the registry enforce quality checks and migration rules. Downstream fixes are duplicated with slightly different logic and unmanaged upstream schema changes break every consumer.
practical_examples: Contract published to Confluent Schema Registry via a platform-team CD task, applied to a Kafka topic (streaming interface), exposed as tables via Tableflow for analytics, derived data products built with Flink.
why_it_matters: Articulates why validation should move toward the producer and how contracts, registries and ownership connect, which informs where a schema framework places enforcement; vendor-promotional for Confluent products.
authority_rationale: Major-vendor engineering blog by a recognised book author; promotional context noted.
notes: Chad Sanderson's 'Shift Left Data Manifesto' was verified only via a secondary trade-press article also fetched: InfoWorld, Andrew C. Oliver, 2025-07-17 (https://www.infoworld.com/article/4023622/it-is-time-to-shift-data-left.html) - contracts 'define shape, semantics, lineage, and ownership', are checked in CI as a merge gate, expectations belong 'inside the code base, not downstream'; example of a one-line change that would have silently dropped 40% of new records caught at check-in in ~30 seconds. The manifesto text itself was not fetched.

title: Apache Iceberg: Branching and Tagging (Audit Branch / Write-Audit-Publish)
core_concepts: Branches and tags as named snapshot references with retention
engineering_principles: Write new data to an audit branch so the main table history is unaffected, validate the branch with data quality checks, then publish by fast-forwarding main to the branch head; retain branches/tags by age and snapshot count; writes to a branch are validated against the current table schema, while tag/snapshot queries use the schema in place at snapshot time.
practical_examples: Six-step audit-branch procedure: enable write.wap.enabled; create an audit branch with e.g. 7-day retention; set spark.wap.branch and run the write; validate; call fast_forward to move main; branch reference removed by expireSnapshots after retention. Historical tags with weekly/monthly/yearly retention; temporary 7-day test branches keeping the latest 2 snapshots.
why_it_matters: The current, vendor-neutral mechanism for the WAP promotion gate at the storage layer, enabling validation before consumers can see data without copying it.
authority_rationale: Official Apache project documentation (Java docs, version 1.12.0).
notes: Body content required reading the page from character offset 100000 because the first segment contained only navigation.

title: Whoops, the Numbers Are Wrong! Scaling Data Quality @ Netflix (Hadoop/DataWorks Summit 2017 slides)
core_concepts: Write-Audit-Publish ETL pattern (Prep, Write, Audit, Publish)
Quinto data quality service with fail/warn rule behaviours
Metacat federated metastore storing extended table attributes (primary keys, lifecycle, audience, valid-thru)
Tiered coverage: not every table needs quality coverage
engineering_principles: Write the new partition to an audit table rather than production, evaluate metrics against configured rules (each rule maps metric + evaluation to fail-the-job or warn), and only then move the partition into the warehouse table; favour modular components over all-or-nothing frameworks; a query-based solution suffices for many use cases.
practical_examples: Row count must be >= 0 and >= prior value (fail on breach); null count compared with a normal distribution (warn), e.g., a jump from 21 to 17,240 nulls flagged; publish step sets a valid-thru timestamp in Metacat; Python libraries 'Jumpstarter' (Quinto) and 'WAP'.
why_it_matters: Primary-source origin of the WAP pattern later built into Iceberg; demonstrates audit metrics, severity tiers and catalog attributes a schema framework can mandate (PK declared in catalog, publish timestamp).
authority_rationale: Major-organisation conference talk by the practitioner who introduced the pattern; slides rather than a peer-reviewed paper.
notes: Related gating case studies: Intuit circuit breakers, Strata SF session 2019-03-27 by Sandeep Uttamchandani (https://conferences.oreilly.com/strata/strata-ca-2019/public/schedule/detail/73082.html, fetched and verified) - 'data availability in dashboards a function of the data quality', inspired by microservices circuit breakers; stage-gating mechanics exist only in a third-party slide copy (not verified). Airbnb 'How Airbnb Built Wall to prevent data bugs' (https://medium.com/airbnb-engineering/how-airbnb-built-wall-to-prevent-data-bugs-ad1b081d6e8f) and 'Data Quality at Airbnb' (https://medium.com/airbnb-engineering/data-quality-at-airbnb-870d03080469): URLs returned verbatim by WebSearch but fetch returned HTTP 403, so url_verified would be false; search snippets indicate Wall is a Python framework on Airflow with config-file checks that can be declared blocking or non-blocking, and Midas certification as a 'gold standard' promise; Part 2 byline suggests Jan 2021 rather than 2020.

title: Databricks: Manage data quality with pipeline expectations (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines)
core_concepts: Expectation = name + SQL boolean constraint + action
Fail (ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE / dp.expect_or_fail; transaction rolled back)
Data quality metrics in the pipeline event log
engineering_principles: Validate each record as it flows through the pipeline with declarative constraints; choose warn to keep rows and record metrics, drop to filter invalid rows, or fail to halt and roll back the update; constraints may not call custom Python, external services or subqueries on other tables; metrics are visible in the Data quality tab or event log.
practical_examples: @dp.expect('valid_timestamp', "timestamp > '2012-01-01'") and CONSTRAINT valid_timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > '2012-01-01'). Companion patterns page (https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectation-patterns, updated 2026-10-26, also fetched): quarantine by computing is_quarantined = NOT(rule1 AND rule2) with @dp.expect_all(rules) and two filtered views (one table with a flag, not a separate physical table); row-count validation materialized view with CONSTRAINT no_rows_dropped EXPECT (a_count == b_count) and fail-on-violation; range validation using mean +/- 3 standard deviations over 30 days with expect_or_drop; caveat that expectations control data quality not orchestration, so blocking downstream work requires separate pipelines linked by a job.
why_it_matters: Official articulation of warn/drop/fail severity tiers, the quarantine pattern and source-to-target row-count reconciliation inside a pipeline, all of which a schema framework can prescribe generically.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation with last-updated dates.
notes: Python examples use the dp namespace (not dlt). Expectations apply only to streaming tables, materialized views and temporary views; not supported with AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT.

title: Kimball Design Tip #164: Have You Built Your Audit Dimension Yet?
core_concepts: Audit dimension attached to fact tables
Environment/version variables (ETL master version, currency-conversion version, allocation version)
Data quality indicator flags (missing data, data supplied/estimated, unlikely value)
Flags sourced from the error event fact table
engineering_principles: Attach an audit dimension to every fact table so business users can see which ETL configuration produced each row and whether quality screens raised warnings; populate version columns from a time-ranged version table and quality flags from the back-room error event schema; keep the design simple initially; flags are warnings, not diagnoses.
practical_examples: Two column groups (environment variables and quality flags); quotes: 'elevates metadata to the status of ordinary data', 'one of the most effective tools for managing data quality and data governance', 'keep it simple and not get too idealistic in the beginning'.
why_it_matters: Provides the dimensional-modelling counterpart to control tables: an audit FK on every fact row that ties quality and provenance to the schema itself, enabling reconciliation and compliance queries.
authority_rationale: Recognised author of the Kimball methodology publishing on the Kimball Group site; foundational practitioner guidance rather than a standard.
notes: Related Kimball Group technique pages also fetched and verified (n.d.): Error Event Schemas (https://www.kimballgroup.com/?p=19414) - data quality screens test data from source systems to the BI platform; error event fact table (one row per error) and error event detail fact table (one row per column per table involved), kept in the ETL back room; Audit Dimension technique page (https://www.kimballgroup.com/?p=19403) - audit attributes include versions of ETL code, useful for compliance and auditing; Late Arriving Facts (https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/late-arriving-fact/) - look up the dimension keys that were effective when the measurement event occurred. The full ETL Toolkit text (screen taxonomy, ABC framework) was not accessible.

title: Oracle Fusion Cloud Financials: Account Reconciliation and Subledgers (Using General Ledger, 26A)
core_concepts: Prerequisite: transactions accounted and journals posted
Exception categories: incomplete accounting, amount mismatch, manual journals, non-subledger journals
Account Analysis report; Payables/Receivables to Ledger Reconciliation reports; Trial Balance
Control accounts restricted to subledger sources
engineering_principles: Compare open subledger balances with the corresponding GL account balance for each accounting period; when they differ, match each subledger transaction to its accounting entry to isolate the cause; designate payables/receivables accounts as control accounts that other sources cannot post to; run reconciliation only after the subledger periods are closed to new transactions; reconcile at ledger or primary balancing segment level; the accounting department owns the process.
practical_examples: Automatic flagging of transactions without complete accounting, amounts that do not tie to the accounting entry, manually entered journals to the account and journals not from the subledger; summary data reflects the extraction run time while detail is real time, so extraction should run after close to minimise discrepancies.
why_it_matters: Authoritative statement of what financial reconciliation requires (control accounts, period-close gating, categorised explained differences), which a schema framework should mandate for financial fact tables and ledgers.
authority_rationale: Official vendor product documentation for a widely used financial system.
notes: The page does not state a numeric zero-difference target; it requires differences to be identified and explained. A linked Receivables-to-GL report page (25A) redirected to a landing page and could not be verified.

title: reladiff - high-performance diffing of large datasets across databases (fork of data-diff)
core_concepts: Cross-database divide-and-conquer hash matching (segment and bisect)
Same-database JOIN-based diff with materialised results
Benchmarks: 25M rows < 10 s; ~1B rows in ~5 min when identical
Dozen+ databases incl. MySQL, Postgres, Snowflake, BigQuery, Oracle, ClickHouse
engineering_principles: Validate replication or migration by comparing checksums of row segments across databases and downloading only mismatching segments, or by joining within one database; materialise diffs for audit.
practical_examples: Cross-database mode for source-to-target verification; same-database mode for before/after comparisons with extra table statistics; Python 3.8+; MIT license.
why_it_matters: Gives the row-level reconciliation technique (hash/segment comparison) that complements count and aggregate controls when exact source-to-target fidelity must be proven.
authority_rationale: Reputable open-source tool README by the maintainer; performance claims are self-reported.
notes: Upstream datafold/data-diff (https://github.com/datafold/data-diff, MIT, also fetched) was archived by its owner on 2024-05-17; Datafold states it is 'no longer actively supporting or developing open source data-diff'. The archived README does not use the terms hashdiff/joindiff.

title: OpenLineage Specification: Object Model (Run, Job, Dataset, facets)
core_concepts: Job (process consuming/producing datasets; unique name per namespace)
Run (instance of a Job; client-generated runId, UUIDv7 recommended)

Facets: job (sourceCodeLocation, sourceCode), run (nominalTime, parent, errorMessage, sql), dataset (schema, dataSource, lifecycleStateChange, version), input (dataQualityMetrics, dataQualityAssertions), output (outputStatistics)
engineering_principles: Emit additive, timestamped run-state events from jobs with their input and output datasets, identified by stable namespace+name, and attach standard or custom facets for schema, SQL, data quality metrics/assertions and output statistics so lineage and quality travel together.
practical_examples: Spec version 1.55.0; example of a scheduled Python script running CREATE TABLE as a Job; Airflow and Spark cited as parent runs. Column lineage facet page (https://openlineage.io/docs/spec/facets/dataset-facets/column_lineage_facet, also fetched): outputs[].facets.columnLineage with fields -> inputFields (namespace, name, field, transformations) where type is DIRECT (IDENTITY, TRANSFORMATION, AGGREGATION) or INDIRECT (JOIN, GROUP_BY, FILTER, SORT, WINDOW, CONDITIONAL) plus a masking boolean; Spark emits it and spark.openlineage.columnLineage.datasetLineageEnabled=True is recommended.
why_it_matters: The open interchange model for run-level and column-level lineage that catalogs (Marquez, DataHub, Dataplex) consume; a schema framework can require stable dataset naming and lineage/quality facet emission from pipelines.
authority_rationale: Specification of an LF AI & Data Foundation Graduate project (confirmed on https://openlineage.io/docs/, also fetched).
notes: Docs home (fetched) lists integrations Airflow, Flink, Hive, Spark, dbt, Feast, Great Expectations, SQL, Trino and names Marquez (https://marquezproject.ai/, fetched; released by WeWork; 'the reference implementation of OpenLineage') and Egeria. Google Dataplex (https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataplex/docs/about-data-lineage, fetched) imports OpenLineage events and recommends that format for custom sources; its API models Process/Run/Event with source-to-target links, automatic lineage from BigQuery (within 24 hours), Managed Airflow, Vertex AI, Data Fusion, Dataproc, Dataflow; column lineage for top-level BigQuery columns only; all lineage retained 30 days.

title: DataHub: Lineage feature guide (table-level and column-level lineage)
core_concepts: Automatic capture via ingestion sources with Table Lineage Capability
Manual UI lineage edits (since v0.9.5) and incremental_lineage flag
engineering_principles: Capture lineage automatically from sources where possible, allow manual or API edges where not, and guard against manual and programmatic edits overwriting each other with incremental_lineage; use lineage for impact analysis and propagation of documentation.
practical_examples: Expand table columns in the lineage view or click a column breadcrumb to focus on one column's lineage; Impact Analysis tool; docs version 1.8.0. Ingestion architecture page (https://docs.datahub.com/docs/architecture/metadata-ingestion, fetched): Metadata Change Proposals over Kafka (async) or synchronous HTTP; pull-based Python ingestion framework schedulable with Airflow; push-based emitters from any system; mce-consumer-job writes to datahub-gms /ingest. Business Glossary page (https://docs.datahub.com/docs/glossary/business-glossary, fetched): Terms and Term Groups with Contains/Inherits From relationships, documentation and unique owners, file-based ingestion on git commit hooks.
why_it_matters: Defines the push vs pull ingestion split and the ownership/glossary primitives a schema framework should feed (owner, description, terms, tags) and shows what column-level lineage looks like in an open catalog.
authority_rationale: Official project documentation; Apache-2.0 project started at LinkedIn in 2019 per the GitHub README (https://github.com/datahub-project/datahub, fetched), which also cites 150+ integrations and observability assertions, freshness checks and incident tracking.
notes: Other open-source catalogs fetched for comparison: OpenMetadata docs v2.0.x (https://docs.open-metadata.org/) - unified discovery, lineage and governance with Dimensional Validation (completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness), Data Quality as Code, data contracts; Apache Atlas (https://github.com/apache/atlas, Apache-2.0) - governance services for Hadoop with lineage, RBAC/ABAC via Apache Ranger and hooks for HBase, Hive, Impala, Kafka, Sqoop, Storm, Falcon, Couchbase; Amundsen (https://github.com/amundsen-io/amundsen, Apache-2.0, LF AI & Data incubation Aug 2020) - repository archived by its owner on 2026-09-29 due to inactivity, and the amundsen.io domain 301-redirected to an unrelated third-party site on 2026-11-07.

title: Databricks: Capture and view data lineage using Unity Catalog
core_concepts: Automatic runtime lineage for Spark DataFrame and Databricks SQL queries
Table-level lineage incl. notebooks, jobs, pipelines, dashboards, ML model versions, file paths
System tables system.access.table_lineage and system.access.column_lineage (rolling 395-day window)
Catalog Explorer lineage retained indefinitely from 2024-09-01
External metadata objects for non-metastore assets
engineering_principles: Lineage is captured automatically for queries on registered Unity Catalog tables and aggregated across workspaces; query it programmatically from system tables; register external sources/consumers (e.g., Salesforce, MySQL, Tableau, Power BI) as external metadata objects with relationships to securables.
practical_examples: Limitations: column lineage not captured for UDFs or path-based references (though column_lineage system table still records path references), renamed catalogs/schemas/tables/views/columns lose lineage, not captured for RDDs, global temp views, dataset checkpointing or information_schema tables, lineage events persist even if a transaction is rolled back, incomplete coverage for Lakeflow pipelines using PRIVATE tables.
why_it_matters: Shows what platform-native lineage can and cannot see, yielding schema-design rules (avoid renames, prefer table references over paths, avoid opaque UDFs) and retention limits that may require export to a catalog.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Lineage captured before 2024-09-01 is unavailable.

title: Snowflake: Data lineage in Snowsight (Horizon Catalog)
core_concepts: Object lineage for tables, dynamic/external/Iceberg tables, views, materialized and semantic views, stages, ML objects, Cortex services
Relationship types: data movement (CTAS, INSERT, MERGE, COPY INTO) and object dependencies
Privileges: VIEW LINEAGE, object privileges or REFERENCES, RESOLVE ALL, QUERY_HISTORY
engineering_principles: Lineage is derived from data-movement statements and object dependencies and exposed per object and per column with a one-year retention; viewing requires account-level VIEW LINEAGE plus object privileges (or REFERENCES to see lineage without data access).
practical_examples: Lineage tab under Catalog > Explorer; column lineage shows upstream/downstream columns and how many steps away each is (not for semantic views). ACCESS_HISTORY page (https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/access-history, also fetched): one record per SQL statement with direct_objects_accessed, base_objects_accessed, objects_modified (write lineage from source columns to target columns for INSERT, MERGE, CTAS), object_modified_by_ddl, policies_referenced; Enterprise Edition; no additional cost for the ACCOUNT_USAGE view.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates column-level lineage derived from query history in a major warehouse and the privilege model needed to expose it; retention (1 year) sets an export requirement for longer audit horizons.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: The lineage page does not itself state that lineage derives from ACCESS_HISTORY; the ACCESS_HISTORY page confirms column-level write lineage in objects_modified, so the link between the two is inferred.

title: Data lineage in classic Microsoft Purview Data Catalog
core_concepts: Lineage as lifecycle from origin across the data estate
Use cases: troubleshooting, root cause, data quality analysis, compliance, impact analysis
Process execution status captured for root-cause and quality scenarios
Catalog connects to processing systems (Data Factory, Synapse, Databricks, Power BI) to extract lineage
engineering_principles: Model lineage as a graph of source and target entities connected by a process invoked by a compute system; capture at the lowest grain each system supports (table rather than partition/file), include ownership and other metadata for human-readable lineage, and record process execution status.
practical_examples: Example chain: Data Factory copies raw data to a landing zone; Synapse/Databricks notebooks transform to curated; analytical models; BI dashboards and ML experiments consume; end-to-end lineage from blob store to Power BI dashboard.
why_it_matters: Gives the canonical three-grain lineage model (entity, column, process execution) that a schema framework can use to specify what pipelines must report.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation (ms.date 2025-02-14; page metadata updated 2025-11-18).
notes: Page is for the classic Data Catalog; the newer Unified Catalog lineage page was not fetched. The URL canonicalises to /purview/data-gov-classic-lineage.

title: Apache Airflow: Best Practices (idempotent tasks, no incomplete results, DAG testing)
core_concepts: Upsert instead of INSERT on re-run
Partition reads by data_interval_start; never read latest data
DAG loader tests, unit tests, self-checks with sensors
engineering_principles: Make every task idempotent so retries and backfills are safe: write with upserts, scope reads and writes to the scheduled data interval, avoid wall-clock dependencies, never leave partial outputs, and test DAGs like production code.
practical_examples: Quotes: 'You should treat tasks in Airflow equivalent to transactions in a database'; 'Do not use INSERT during a task re-run'; 'Never read the latest available data in a task'. Airflow 3.4.0 docs. Companion common-sql provider page (https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow-providers-common-sql/stable/operators.html, provider 2.4.0, also fetched): SQLColumnCheckOperator (null_check, distinct_check, unique_check, min, max with tolerance and partition clauses), SQLTableCheckOperator (boolean check_statement such as COUNT(*) = 1), SQLValueCheckOperator (pass_value with tolerance), SQLThresholdCheckOperator (min/max thresholds; task fails outside them).
why_it_matters: Idempotent, partition-scoped loads are the precondition for safe re-runs after a failed audit or reconciliation, and orchestrator check operators provide the pipeline-level gate that fails the task (and thus downstream work) on violation.
authority_rationale: Official Apache project documentation.
notes: The best-practices page does not mention SQL check operators or a write-to-temp-then-move pattern; the operators page does not describe SQLCheckOperator or SQLIntervalCheckOperator.

title: Debezium connector for PostgreSQL - Monitoring (streaming and snapshot metrics)
core_concepts: Snapshot metrics: SnapshotRunning/Completed/Aborted, RowsScanned, RemainingTableCount, incremental chunk bounds
engineering_principles: Monitor CDC health by lag between source commit time and connector processing time (noting host clock skew), time since last event, connectivity, queue saturation and error counts; export via JMX to Prometheus/Grafana.
practical_examples: MilliSecondsBehindSource description: 'Gap between the last change event's timestamp and when the connector processed it. Clock differences between the database and connector hosts affect this value'; percentile metrics available when statistics.metrics.enabled is true (default). Debezium 3.7 documentation; operations/monitoring page (https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/operations/monitoring.html, also fetched) covers JMX setup and best-effort Grafana dashboards.
why_it_matters: Provides the concrete metrics for freshness/lag SLOs on CDC feeds that a schema framework can require to be monitored for replicated tables.
authority_rationale: Official project documentation.
notes: Monitoring section was read from character offset 250000 of the connector page. The page names the queue metric QueueTotalCapacity, not QueueTotalSize.

title: PostgreSQL 18: COMMENT - define or change the comment of an object
core_concepts: COMMENT ON TABLE / COLUMN / CONSTRAINT / VIEW / SCHEMA / DATABASE / DOMAIN / FUNCTION / POLICY / TRIGGER and others
One comment per object; new COMMENT replaces; NULL or empty string removes
Viewing via psql \d family and obj_description / col_description / shobj_description
Visibility: any user connected to the database can see all comments
engineering_principles: Store table and column descriptions in the database catalog alongside the DDL so documentation travels with the schema and can be harvested by catalogs; never place sensitive information in comments because they are visible to every connected user.
practical_examples: COMMENT ON TABLE my_schema.my_table IS 'Employee Information'; COMMENT ON COLUMN my_table.my_column IS 'Employee ID number'; COMMENT ON TABLE mytable IS NULL to remove.
why_it_matters: Establishes the OLTP mechanism for the design-time requirement that every table and column carries a description, which catalog ingestion (pull) can then surface.
authority_rationale: Official PostgreSQL documentation (PostgreSQL 18).
notes: Page does not mention \d+ or pg_description explicitly; those are general PostgreSQL knowledge.
